blocks.text: Dissolving a solute in a solvent is dissolution. The formation of a solution is assumed to take three steps: overcoming the intermolecular forces in the solvent to make room for the solute (expanding the solvent), breaking the solute into individual components (expanding the solute), and letting solute and solvent interact to form the solution. Heat is either given out or taken in, and the standard enthalpy change of solution describes it.

blocks.title: Standard enthalpy change of solution
blocks.text: The standard enthalpy of solution, delta Hsol, is the heat absorbed or evolved when one mole of a substance is dissolved in a solvent to give an infinitely dilute solution. It may be exothermic or endothermic.

Sodium carbonate dissolves exothermically, Na2CO3(s) + aq gives 2Na+(aq) + CO3 2-(aq), delta Hsol = -25 kJ per mol; ammonium chloride endothermically, NH4Cl(s) + aq gives NH4+(aq) + Cl-(aq), delta Hsol = +16.2 kJ per mol. The magnitude of the heat of solution tells about the strength of the intermolecular forces between the components that mix. An ionic compound consists of oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces, and two factors govern its dissolution: the hydration energy, the attraction of the solute ions to water molecules, and the lattice energy, which controls the breaking up of the ionic compound.
